newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Five powers affirm U.S. security presence in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Five powers affirm U.S. security presence in Asia.

text.p: Defence ministers from five nations on Tuesday welcomed a U.S. security presence in Asia and Britain's commitment to deploy its navy more frequently in the region after handing Hong Kong back to China.

Ministers representing the Five Power Defence Arrangement (FPDA) met as elements of their armed forces staged a two-week air and naval exercise off Malaysia's east coast, one of the biggest held in Southeast Asia.

The FPDA, formed 26 years ago during the Vietnam War, requires Britain, Australia and New Zealand to consult with Singapore and Malaysia in the event of an external crisis facing the two Southeast Asian nations.
All five are members of the Commonwealth.

Malaysian Defence Minister Syed Hamid Albar told reporters the meeting, held every three years, reaffirmed the role of the FPDA in the external defence of Malaysia and Singapore and discussed various security issues in Asia.
"We looked at our perceptions of the security environment or framework of the area," Syed Hamid said. "We see the need of the U.S. continued presence."

Although the United States closed its air and naval bases in the Philippines several years ago, it still maintains about 100,000 troops in South Korea and Japan. U.S. warships also frequently call on ports in Asia.
The ministers welcomed Britain's decision to deploy its navy more frequently in the region after the handover of Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30.

"We appreciate the British undertaking they will deploy on a more frequent basis their naval forces and they will continue with bilateral and multilateral exercises" after the handover and the loss of naval base in Hong Kong, he added.
"I think in the case of Britain, because they are the main party..., to them they consider the FPDA the core platform for their military involvement in the region," Syed Hamid said.
Because the presence of foreign bases had become such a sensitive issue in many countries "you have to find new approaches, new ways of having access", he said.
"I think in our case having access means joint exercises, having common facilities, bringing commonality in terms of our assets or command and control and communications.
"That's why we talk about inter-operability as being the key factor that will ensure effectiveness of the countries in the new security environment of the region as well as the globe.
"At the end of the day you cannot sustain bases so you have to be able to access places more quickly. So the air and the navy play an important part in this new security environment."
The FPDA's 13-day mock air and sea battle began off Malaysia's Tioman Island in the South China Sea on Monday.
Codenamed "Flying Fish 97", it involves 12,000 members of the armed forces from the five nations, 160 fighter jets, 39 ships -- including a British aircraft carrier -- and two submarines.
Britain is contributing much of the muscle with 16 ships, including the aircraft carrier HMS Illustrious.

Australia's Defence Minister Ian McLachlan, New Zealand Defence Minister Paul East, Singapore's Defence Minister Tony Tan and British parliamentary under-secretary of state for defence the Earl Howe were also at the FPDA meeting.
Hamid said other issues discussed included recent tensions in the Taiwan Strait and on the Korean Peninsula as well as the overlapping claims to the Spratly Islands.
A string of islands in the South China Sea, the Spratlys are claimed in whole or in part by China, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
"We have expressed our satisfaction that China is engaged in constructive dialogue and even the U.S. has engaged China in discussions," Syed Hamid said.
